nameStory: Little-leaf tick-clover gets its name from two key features that any hiker will remember after an encounter. The 'tick' part comes from its sticky seed pods that grab onto your clothes and socks just like ticks do, hitching a ride to new places. The 'little-leaf' part distinguishes it from its bigger-leafed cousins in the tick-trefoil family.
description: Little-leaf tick-clover is a modest wildflower that stands about knee-high in New England's woodlands and clearings. This perennial grows anywhere from 8 inches to 3 feet tall, with a slender, upright stem that often has a slightly fuzzy texture. Like all members of the legume family, it has three-part leaves (called trifoliolate) arranged alternately up the stem, and produces small pink or purple pea-like flowers. It's the kind of plant you might overlook until its clingy seeds remind you it was there all along.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three small leaflets per leaf, each oval-shaped and notably smaller than other tick-trefoils, with tiny hairs along the edges that you can feel if you run your finger gently along the margin

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink or purple pea-shaped flowers clustered loosely along the upper stem, each flower about the size of your pinky fingernail

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, segmented seed pods that break apart into triangular pieces covered in tiny hooked hairs that grab onto fabric and fur with surprising tenacity

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, upright stem that feels slightly rough and hairy to the touch, often growing in small colonies from underground runners

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Notably hairy stem with fine, soft bristles that catch the light when viewed from the side, giving it a slightly fuzzy appearance

habitat: Look for little-leaf tick-clover in partially shaded areas like woodland edges, forest clearings, and along trails where the canopy lets in some dappled sunlight. It prefers well-drained, slightly acidic soils and often grows alongside other woodland wildflowers and young trees. You'll commonly find it in areas that have been disturbed by logging or trail maintenance, where it can take advantage of the increased light.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with fresh three-part leaves that are bright green and noticeably soft to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with small pink or purple flowers appearing from mid to late summer, typically July through August.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and become incredibly sticky, readily attaching to clothing and animal fur for dispersal. Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving only the underground root system, though you might still find old seed pods clinging to dried stems.

funFact: The sticky seed pods are so effective at hitchhiking that they inspired part of the design for Velcro - the tiny hooked hairs grab onto fabric loops with a grip so strong that Native Americans traditionally used the plants to remove splinters by pressing the sticky pods against their skin.
confusionNotes: It's easily confused with other tick-trefoils, but remember 'little-leaf' - this species has noticeably smaller leaflets than its relatives. If the three leaflets are each smaller than a quarter, you're likely looking at little-leaf tick-clover rather than the larger showy or tall tick-trefoils.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'clover,' tick-trefoils aren't true clovers at all - they're just distant cousins in the huge legume family. True clovers have their flowers bunched into round heads, while tick-trefoils have flowers arranged more loosely along the stem.
compareHints: Among its tick-trefoil relatives, little-leaf stands out for its distinctly smaller leaflets and notably hairy stems. While showy tick-trefoil can grow 4 feet tall with large leaflets, and tall tick-trefoil has smooth stems, little-leaf stays more modest in size with fuzzy stems and leaflets that are typically less than an inch long.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its tick-trefoil relatives, showy tick-trefoil is typically the tallest and most robust, with the largest and most densely packed flower clusters.

Among New England's many ticktrefoils, panicled ticktrefoil stands out with its distinctly narrow, lance-shaped leaflets - much thinner than the broad leaflets of showy tick-trefoil or the rounded leaves of round-leaved trailing tick-trefoil.
Among the tick-trefoils, this is the only one with perfectly round leaflets and a distinctly trailing growth habit.
Among the tick-trefoils, this species stands out for its height and smooth appearance.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, Maryland tick-trefoil is distinguished by its relatively small, smooth leaflets and delicate overall appearance.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, perplexed tick-trefoil is most easily confused with tall tick-trefoil, requiring expert examination to separate reliably.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, the toothed variety stands out for its distinctly serrated leaf edges - most other species have smooth or only slightly toothed leaflets.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, hoary tick-trefoil is the gray ghost - its fuzzy, grayish appearance makes it unmistakable.
Among New England's ticktrefoils, sessileleaf is the only one with leaves that attach directly to the stem without stalks - all its relatives have obvious leaf stems.
Among the tick-trefoils, stiff tick-trefoil stands out for its rigid, unbending stems - most others like showy tick-trefoil or panicled tick-trefoil have flexible stems that sway easily.
